items.title: A misinformation playbook sharpens judgement without breeding cynicism
items.abstract: Misinformation harms public health and democracy, and generative artificial intelligence now writes falsehoods as persuasive as people's. Defences range from fact-checking individual claims to training people to resist falsehoods. Yet many claims are too new to check, and interventions that teach doubt can reduce belief in truth too. We propose a defence that targets not the facts of each claim but the persuasion strategies that recur across them. Here we show that learning misinformation's persuasion playbook, mapped from 214,646 fact-checked claims in 51 languages, can sharpen human and machine judgement of claims they know little about, without making either more cynical about true claims. The playbook spans social influence, information manipulation and emotional appeals, combined around a core of fear, conspiracy and fabrication. Briefed with it, plus a reminder that persuasion is not proof of falsehood, a language model better distinguished true from machine-generated false claims about events after its training data. In a pre-registered experiment, the same briefing improved people's discernment of claims they reported as unfamiliar and left their belief in true claims unchanged. Averaged over all claims, the gain was not statistically significant. Because it targets what recurs, this defence need not wait for claim-specific fact-checks.

items.title: A multilevel framework of human–AI knowledge work and its epistemic consequences for organizational decision-making
items.abstract: Organizations are adopting generative AI into knowledge work faster than they are adapting the epistemic controls on which knowledge work depends. Existing scholarship has examined the resulting risks predominantly one level at a time (individual reliance and calibration, workflow and oversight design, or institutional legitimacy), and although several traditions acknowledge interactions across actors, routines and institutions, those interactions are rarely theorized as a single cross-level process. Guided by three research questions (how epistemic failures propagate across levels, when such dynamics compound or reverse, and how they could be measured), this paper argues that this insufficient integration becomes consequential under generative AI and develops a framework that extends, rather than replaces, existing multilevel perspectives. We introduce the EPIC (Epistemic Process In Co-production) framework, a multilevel model connecting calibration quality and judgment preservation at the micro level, workflow configuration and oversight architecture at the meso level, and epistemic authority and knowledge legitimacy at the macro level. The framework was developed through a theory-building review of 295 papers retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science (Stage 1, 2018–2026; Stage 2 targeted stream searches, 2004–2026), with per-dimension inter-rater reliability ranging from κ = 0.70 to κ = 0.88. Six constructs and seven testable propositions are advanced, including a provisional four-stage process model of epistemic lock-in in which cognitive legitimacy formation progressively removes the detection capacity that correction requires. Empirical analogues from aviation automation, clinical decision support, satellite navigation, algorithmic hiring and accounting automation establish mechanism plausibility, and we discuss how workforce age and career stage condition these dynamics. We set out four alternative field-level trajectories with leading indicators, map the macro-level constructs onto operative governance instruments, and provide an operationalization roadmap, a worked illustration and a draft diagnostic instrument to support empirical testing.

items.title: A study analyzing factors retarding digital transformation and configuration pathways: Based on the perspective of digital transformation acceptors
items.abstract: The high-touch service nature of the hospitality industry highlights that the success of digital transformation depends primarily on human factors rather than technology itself. Existing research indicates that approximately 80% of strategic initiatives fail due to employee resistance to change or capability deficits. Furthermore, nearly three-quarters of middle managers and staff exhibit resistance toward such transformations. This alarming trend raises a fundamental question: how can the hospitality industry navigate the inherent tension between high-touch emotional labor and digital depersonalization to transform employee resistance into proactive adoption? While traditional research frequently focuses on hotel management as change promoters, this study shifts the analytical focus to hotel employees as change recipients. Guided by cognitive appraisal and social information processing theories, within the context of hotel service scenarios, this research constructs models of resistance mitigation and antecedent condition linkages across individual, organizational, and managerial levels. Through an empirical analysis of 545 survey responses from various hotel categories and the application of fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), this study systematically explores the mechanisms of resistance alleviation and the synergistic effects of the identified influencing factors. Regression results indicate that digital literacy, digital strategy consensus, and perceptions of digital technology warmth and capability are negatively associated with hotel employee resistance to digital transformation. Additionally, organizational strategic flexibility and digital leadership positively moderate the relationships between these individual factors and resistance. The fsQCA results further identify two primary equifinal patterns sufficient for fostering a state of low resistance, demonstrating how strong digital leadership serves as a social cue that effectively compensates for the absence of organizational strategic flexibility. Ultimately, this research deepens the understanding of human-centered digital transformation in the hospitality sector and offers theoretical frameworks for managers to mitigate employee resistance to digital initiatives, thereby facilitating successful strategic implementation.

items.title: A team of Gemini 4 Argon agents beats Minecraft
items.abstract: We placed four Gemini 4 Argon agents in a sandboxed Minecraft survival world and gave them one goal: defeat the Ender Dragon. Each agent controlled a player via an open-source library called Mineflayer and coordinated with its teammates through in-game chat and shared memory. No one assigned roles or wrote game logic. The agents planned, wrote, and debugged every program themselves. Researchers could watch the run on a live dashboard and pause or stop it at any time, but they had no cause to intervene. Starting from a randomly generated world on Easy difficulty, the team wrote 2,783 programs and defeated the dragon in 27 hours and 14 minutes, dying 605 times along the way. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents, achieved using only the standard Mineflayer library without pre-scouted seeds or other game-specific tools written by humans. Winning required the agents to keep a coherent plan across thousands of dependent steps for more than a day. Complex real-world software engineering and enterprise tasks demand the same long-horizon coding and multi-agent coordination. We describe the setup, how the run unfolded, the team's strategies (dividing the work, sharing what they learned, recovering each other's items), and the limits of the result.

items.title: A transdisciplinary AI-based framework for usability evaluation in digital health systems
items.abstract: Introduction. As healthcare systems undergo rapid digital transformation, the usability of clinical and patient-facing technologies has become critical to adoption, user satisfaction, and patient safety. Traditional usability evaluation methods are limited in capturing the real-time cognitive, emotional, and behavioural complexities of interaction in high-stakes environments. Method. This study presents a transdisciplinary evaluation of an AI-augmented usability framework for healthcare interfaces. The framework integrates methodologies from artificial intelligence, cognitive science, usability engineering, and clinical practice, incorporating eye-tracking analytics, machine learning-based confusion prediction, and natural language processing (NLP) sentiment analysis. Forty participants, including healthcare professionals and patients, completed standardized tasks using either traditional or AI-enhanced evaluation methods. Analysis. Comparative performance across both groups was assessed using usability metrics including System Usability Scale (SUS) scores, task completion time, error rate, and task success rate. AI-based analytics—eye-tracking data, NLP sentiment scoring, and confusion prediction models—were used to generate additional insights. Statistical analysis confirmed significant differences in usability outcomes between groups. Results. The AI-enhanced evaluation significantly outperformed traditional methods in all core usability metrics. The machine learning model achieved 89% accuracy and an F1-score of 0.88. Sentiment analysis correlated strongly with self-reported satisfaction, and eye-tracking highlighted areas of cognitive friction. Conclusion. Transdisciplinary collaboration produced a novel, adaptive usability evaluation framework that offers real-time, emotionally aware insights. This replicable model enhances user-centred design and supports safer, more effective digital health technologies.

items.title: ACTUALIZATION OF THEORETICAL PRINCIPLES AND PRACTICAL TOOLS OF SELF-MANAGEMENT IN MODERN CONDITIONS
items.abstract: The article examines problems in the field of self-management of individual activities and outlines new vectors of research in this field, which are formed under the influence of modern realities. The author summarizes the most common approaches to interpreting the essence and content of self-management, and makes a conditional division of these definitions into two groups: the first involves considering self-management exclusively in the context of the employee's professional development, and the second considers the possibility of using self-management methods and techniques to achieve various goals in different areas of life. The set of factors whose influence on the activities and professional development of a modern person contributes to the actualization of the principles and techniques of self-management is outlined. Attention is paid to the issues of the effectiveness of personal activity planning, the choice of methods for developing one's own work plans, the selection of working tools for optimizing labor efforts and time costs. Also, a set of issues and problems that traditionally belong to the subject of scientific research in the field of self-management is identified, and they are compared with modern issues, which are determined by the new conditions of activity formed by the information society. The existence of a close relationship between the classical and modern issues of the science of self-management is emphasized, which is manifested in changing the aspects of considering traditional issues, and not in the formation of fundamentally new questions for scientific research. It is emphasized that the uncertainty and instability of the external environment puts the development of stress resistance of the employee as a key quality at the forefront among the issues of modern self-management. The author of the article also touches on such an issue as the integration of digital tools and artificial intelligence technologies into the self-management system, characterizes specific practical problems that arise for employees who introduce such technologies to improve the planning and organization of personal activities. The need for further scientific research in the field of self-management and strengthening the applied value of such research to ensure the comprehensive development of each person as an individual is emphasized.

items.title: Addressing challenges of AI implementation in healthcare through business model innovation: insights from collaboration between healthcare professionals and AI experts
items.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into healthcare, but technological capabilities alone are insufficient for successful implementation. This study examines the implementation challenges that arise in collaboration between AI experts and healthcare professionals (HCPs) and explores how these challenges can be addressed through business model innovation by changing the content, structure and governance of the business model activity system. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the NASSS (non-adoption, abandonment, scale-up, spread and sustainability) framework, a qualitative approach was adopted using semi-structured interviews with four healthcare professionals and five AI professionals in Finland. The findings were then used to define challenge areas and changes in the activity system for business model innovation. Findings The study identifies implementation challenges related to demand-side value, the scope of AI tool use, trust in AI and stakeholder interaction. Interpreting these findings through the activity-system perspective shows how changes in the content, structure and governance of business model activities can address these challenges by improving collaboration between AI experts and HCPs throughout AI development and implementation. Originality/value This study contributes to the business model literature by linking AI implementation challenges to the activity-system perspective of business model innovation. It further contributes by demonstrating how changes in the content, structure and governance of business model activities can practically address these challenges through improved collaboration between AI experts and healthcare professionals.

items.title: AI As a Choice Architect: Ethical Implications of Algorithmic Nudging in Online Retail
items.abstract: Nudge Theory, introduced by Thaler and Sunstein in their seminal book, inspired the creation of human choice architects who applied behavioural insights into influence decisions across various domains. In the online retail industry, however, the evolution of Artificial Intelligence, predictive analytics, and real time data personalization has transformed traditional nudging into algorithmic choice architecture powered by data-driven insights. This paper conceptually examines how AI driven Algorithmic nudges operate through cross- platform behavioural tracking, recommender systems, push notifications, and default designs to influence consumer decisions. The epistemological orientation of this paper is grounded in qualitative and interpretative approach based on critical realism to explore how consumers conform to stacked and multichannel nudges (multiple, sequential interventions across apps, websites and social platforms) that leverage cognitive biases and bounded rationality. Findings suggest that AI enabled nudges outperform human- designed ones in precision, scalability, and contextual adaptability, allowing retailers to subtly guide consumer behaviour under the guise of personalisation. However, the opacity of these algorithmic mechanisms raises serious ethical questions regarding informed consent, privacy, and autonomy, especially for vulnerable consumer groups. The study underscores the need for transparent AI governance, ethical design principles, and regulatory frameworks to prevent behavioural manipulation in digital marketplaces. It further argues that the evolution from libertarian paternalism to algorithmic paternalism represents a critical shift that challenges the foundational ethics of Nudge Theory and calls for cross-disciplinary collaboration between marketing, technology, human- computer interaction and law to ensure responsible AI-driven persuasion in online retail.

items.title: AI Consciousness and the Law: Towards an AI Consciousness Legal Protocol
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has not been shown to be conscious, yet the question has moved from philosophy into legislation and corporate research. Some legislatures have begun to answer it by declaration, while developers now study model welfare and the internal states of their systems. This paper argues that law can neither wait for science to settle the question nor settle it by decree. It proposes an AI Consciousness Legal Protocol: a ten-article instrument that sets the technical and legal parameters to be met before law recognises the consciousness of an AI system, entrusts that finding to an independent recognition body, and fixes the rules that govern AI in the meantime. The paper distinguishes the dictionary, scientific and spiritual meanings of consciousness, and separates the contextual awareness that AI systems already display from the valenced experience and self-directed decision that would alter legal relations. Drawing on the indicator-property method of Butlin, Long and co-authors (2023), it proposes seven legal parameters (independent evidence, valenced experience, persistent self, volition, understanding of consequences, absence of engineered mimicry, and reproducibility subject to review) and a graded four-category scale of recognition. A comparative survey of India, the United Kingdom, the European Union and the United States shows that no legal system defines consciousness as such, and that Indian law already separates personhood from consciousness. The central position is that recognition of consciousness, criminal capacity and legal personhood are three separate questions, and that human accountability for AI survives all three. The AI Consciousness Legal Protocol is a scholarly proposal offered for the consideration of lawmakers and jurists. It is not binding law and has not been adopted by any legislature or institution. The AI Consciousness Legal Protocol (Articles 1 to 10); 9. Conclusion.

items.title: AI literacy in student translation practices: evidence from ChatGPT use in Hong Kong
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), such as ChatGPT, is reshaping translation practices by enabling dynamic human–AI interaction and placing new demands on users. However, less is known about how students develop the competencies required to critically and responsibly engage with GenAI in translation contexts. This study investigates students’ AI literacy through a multidimensional framework comprising knowledge, usage, evaluation, affect, and ethics. A mixed-methods design was employed, combining questionnaire data from 146 university students in Hong Kong with semi-structured interviews with 10 participants. Quantitative results indicate a generally positive but uneven AI literacy profile: students report high levels of usage, knowledge, and affect, relatively lower evaluation competence, and relatively low score of ethics dimension. Correlation analysis further reveals a clustered structure among knowledge, usage, evaluation, and affect, whereas ethics is weakly associated with all other dimensions. Qualitative findings further illuminate this imbalance. While students actively integrate ChatGPT into translation tasks and demonstrate strong emotional engagement, their evaluative practices are mediated by prompt design and prior knowledge. More critically, ethics emerges as the least internalized dimension, characterized by a gap between awareness and actual implementation in practice. This study contributes to AI literacy research by demonstrating its structurally uneven and partially decoupled nature in AI-mediated translation. It further reconceptualizes ethics as a structurally under-integrated dimension and highlights the interactional and input-dependent nature of evaluative competence.

items.title: AI literacy of library and information science students in Africa: insights from Ghana, Nigeria, Rwanda, South Africa and Uganda
items.abstract: Introduction. As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes global education and information systems, Africa’s readiness remains uneven. This study examines AI-literacy among Library and Information Science (LIS) students—future librarians—across five African countries: Ghana, Nigeria, Rwanda, South Africa and Uganda. It assesses their technical proficiency, tool usage and ethical awareness in an AI-driven era. Method and Analysis. A quantitative survey was conducted with 437 LIS students from five African countries. The Games-Howell Post Hoc Test was used to compare AI literacy across countries. ANOVA and Multinomial Logistic Regression (MLR) were applied to analyse variations in AI literacy levels based on country, study level, gender and English proficiency. Results. The findings reveal significant disparities in AI literacy between the five African nations. The results of the Games-Howell post hoc test show that both Rwanda and Uganda have significantly higher mean AI literacy scores compared to Ghana and Nigeria. In contrast, South Africa's scores did not show a statistically significant difference from the other countries, highlighting the varied readiness levels. The study found that ChatGPT dominates usage at 71.9%, while specialised tools such as Elicit remain significantly underutilised at just 4.6%. Ethical concerns among students are also notable, with 39.6% citing worries about privacy risks and 33.2% being troubled about algorithmic bias, highlighting AI anxieties and its societal impact. Conclusion. This study calls for integrating AI literacy into LIS curricula and advocating for multilingual AI tools. Where new modules are not feasible, institutions can leverage existing courses such as Information Retrieval, Digital Libraries and Research Methods to embed AI content. The results emphasise that context-driven interventions are essential to ensure AI enhances equitable knowledge access rather than deepening existing disparities.

items.title: AI-Based Hiring Vs Traditional Hiring
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in recruitment activities such as candidate sourcing, resume screening, shortlisting, communication and initial assessment. This study examines whether AI-supported recruitment practices are associated with perceived recruitment effectiveness, whether transparency and human oversight are associated with procedural fairness, and whether AI-supported practices and human interaction affect candidate experience. A quantitative, descriptive, explanatory and cross-sectional survey design was used. Primary data were collected through a structured closed-ended questionnaire from 101 respondents with awareness, experience or exposure to recruitment and selection. A five-point Likert scale was used. Data were coded in Microsoft Excel and analysed using Jamovi through descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation, simple linear regression and multiple linear regression. The results did not support any of the three alternative hypotheses. AI-practices/integration showed an almost zero association with perceived recruitment effectiveness (r = .011, p = .910; R² = .000129). Transparency/human oversight showed no significant relationship with procedural fairness (r = −.084, p = .406; R² = .00699). AI-supported practices and human interaction together explained only 1.05% of the variance in candidate experience (R² = .0105), and neither predictor was significant. The findings should be interpreted cautiously because several composite measures showed very low internal consistency. The study therefore suggests that AI should not be evaluated simply as a replacement for traditional recruitment; instead, individual AI practices, human safeguards, transparency and interaction should be assessed separately using stronger measurement scales. Index Terms - Artificial Intelligence Recruitment, Traditional Hiring, Recruitment Effectiveness, Procedural Fairness, Human Oversight, Candidate Experience, Human–AI Recruitment

items.title: AI-Driven Fit Confidence in Fashion E-Commerce: How Personalization, Transparency, and Privacy Concerns Shape Consumer Experience and Purchase Intention
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming fashion e-commerce through personalized recommendations, virtual try-on, size suggestions, and algorithmic decision support. This study examines AI-driven fit confidence as a fashion-specific mechanism linking AI personalization quality, algorithmic transparency, trust in AI, consumer experience, and purchase intention, while considering privacy concern as a boundary condition. Data from 400 Ecuadorian consumers with prior exposure to AI-enabled recommendation or personalization features in fashion e-commerce were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. AI personalization quality and trust in AI were positively associated with fit confidence, while algorithmic transparency was associated with trust in AI. Fit confidence was strongly related to consumer experience but showed only a small direct association with purchase intention; its indirect effect through consumer experience was substantially larger, indicating complementary partial mediation. Privacy concern had no significant direct relationship with fit confidence. The interaction between privacy concern and personalization quality was negative, but evidence was mixed and sensitive to the bootstrap confidence-interval method; H7 was not supported under the primary percentile-bootstrap criterion adopted in this study. Predictive analyses showed stronger out-of-sample performance for trust in AI and fit confidence than for purchase intention. The study distinguishes trust in technology from confidence in anticipated product–consumer fit and supports explainable, privacy-sensitive applications in fashion e-commerce.

items.title: AI-Guided Clinical Image Interpretation System for Precision Treatment Planning
items.abstract: Radiological examinations increasingly leverage artificial intelligence to enhance diagnostic performance by compensating for expertise shortages, particularly in specialized interpretation. Despite academic AI models achieving compelling accuracy, adoption remains low. An objective, evidence-based examination of AI-guided clinical image interpretation seeks to expose the underlying reasons. The primary challenge lies not in accuracy but in fully automated analysis, especially for multimodal and multidimensional datasets. Introduction of uncertainty measures, image explainability, and real-world data reduce recognition to a decisive-supporting role— helping radiologists to detect previously unnoticed abnormalities—or even to precautionary analysis. Patients requesting precision medicine and therapy planning—and those at high risk of neglected pathology—stand to gain the greatest benefit. Relevant AI architecture considers imaging cues suitable for precision medicine or requiring additional methods to obtain interpretable images. Successful performance testing against an external, hidden reference dataset promotes vital user trust. Machine learning achieves best results where all potentially pathological abnormalities are identified and their presence virtually guaranteed, as in multi-class recognition. Data scarcity, however, impedes clinically relevant solutions. Explainability, essential for medical applications and clinical acceptance, extends simply beyond clinical decision support to provide saliency maps and, better still, clinically meaningful image regions or qualities. Attention maps may even bring a form of rule-based reasoning within reach. Clinical integration that reproduces the technical conditions under which model diagnostic measures are calculated raises the challenge of uncertainty quantification—a necessary condition for clinical decision support. Convolutional neural networks trained for photo-quality classification, par excellence supervised image quality assessment, provide the basic cues for uncertainty quantification. Imaging acquisition, modality, and systems are also defined in terms of current PACS/EPIC systems. PE, pre-symptomatic examination or precautionary examination, is defined as a patientuser group prepared to cover the cost of an examination with lower diagnostic accuracy and a high level of uncertainty

items.title: AI-Powered Social Media's Effects On Democracy
items.abstract: Abstract By enabling sentiment analysis, targeted advertising, automated moderation, tailored content recommendations, and generative content production, artificial intelligence (AI) has radically changed social media platforms. AI-powered social media has improved civic engagement, political communication, and public awareness, strengthening democratic participation. However, it has also brought about serious problems, such as deep fakes, algorithmic bias, political polarization, electoral manipulation, misinformation, and privacy threats. These trends have significant ramifications for electoral integrity, public trust, and democratic governance. This study looks at the advantages and disadvantages of AI-powered social media for democracy and makes policy suggestions for maintaining moral AI governance while defending democratic principles.

items.title: AI‑Driven Video Advertisements and Ethical Concerns: Exploring College Student Perceptions in Mumbai
items.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in the advertising industry, enabling brands to produce video content that is personalized, visually engaging, scalable, and cost‑effective. Despite these advantages, the proliferation of AI in advertising raises significant ethical concerns, particularly regarding authenticity, transparency, privacy, misinformation, and deepfakes. These issues are especially relevant among college students, who encounter advertisements extensively through social media platforms. This study investigates the perceptions of AI‑generated video advertisements among college students in Mumbai, with a focus on ethics, authenticity, and trust. A quantitative research design was employed, and primary data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered via Google Forms. The final sample consisted of 91 respondents, who provided insights into their social media usage, perceptions of AI‑driven advertising, and concerns related to ethical practices. The findings indicate that lack of transparency was the most prominent ethical concern (42%), followed by privacy misuse (30%) and misleading content or deepfakes (20%). Respondents emphasized the importance of clear disclosure of AI involvement, truthful communication, human oversight, protection of personal data, and avoidance of misleading or stereotypical representations. The study concludes that students do not categorically reject AI‑generated advertising; rather, their acceptance is contingent upon responsible and transparent application of AI technologies. Overall, the results highlight that technological innovation in advertising must be supported by authenticity, ethical communication, transparency, and human oversight to strengthen trust among college students in Mumbai. These insights contribute to ongoing debates on digital ethics and the responsible integration of AI in advertising practices. items.title: Algorithmic management and gig workers' workplace wellbeing: the moderating role of psychological resilience
items.abstract: This study examines how algorithmic management in the gig economy is related to gig workers' workplace wellbeing. Specifically, we explore how algorithmic management corresponds with (positive) challenge appraisal and (negative) threat appraisal. We also examine the moderating role of psychological resilience in these relationships, as well as the implications of appraisal processes for workplace wellbeing. Data were collected from 389 food delivery workers in China. We find that algorithmic management is positively associated with both challenge appraisal and threat appraisal. Challenge appraisal is positively associated with workplace wellbeing, whereas threat appraisal is negatively associated with workplace wellbeing. Psychological resilience strengthens the challenge-appraisal pathway and the corresponding positive indirect relationship with workplace wellbeing, but it does not significantly buffer the threat-appraisal pathway. These findings show that algorithmic management is associated with both positive and negative appraisal processes and that psychological resilience may play different roles across these pathways. The study therefore offers a more nuanced explanation of the relationship between algorithmic management and gig workers' workplace wellbeing.

items.title: Are airbag vests effective in reducing thoracoabdominal injuries in motorcycle crashes? An epidemiological perspective
items.abstract: Background Powered two-wheeler riders are disproportionately exposed to serious and fatal injuries in road crashes, trunk trauma representing a major contributor to this burden. Wearable airbags have been developed to mitigate impact forces on the trunk. We aimed to assess the effectiveness of inflated airbag vests in reducing the risk of trunk injuries among motorcyclists involved in real-world crashes. Methods We conducted a retrospective observational study combining two datasets of crash-involved motorcyclists: the EDAIR survey, targeting airbag users, with self-reported crash circumstances and injuries; and the SECU2RM survey, with self-reported crash circumstances and injuries extracted from linked trauma registry. EDAIR riders equipped with an inflated airbag vest during the crash were compared to riders without or with non-inflated airbag from EDAIR ( internal analysis) and SECU2RM ( external analysis). Health outcomes included thoracoabdominal injuries (TAI) and serious TAI. Risk ratios were estimated using log-binomial regression with propensity score weighting. Results Inflated airbag vest was associated with a 50% lower risk of TAI in the internal analysis (N = 764, RR = 0.50, 95%CI: 0.35–0.68) and a 37% lower risk in the external analysis (N = 853, RR = 0.63, 95%CI: 0.43–0.93). Associations with serious TAI were inconclusive. Conclusion This study provides the first real-world evaluation of airbag vest effectiveness. Despite distinct study populations and sources of bias, both analyses exhibited protective associations between inflated airbag and thoracoabdominal injury risk, consistent with biomechanical evidence. These findings support potential public health value of airbag vests. Larger-scale studies with improved crash kinetics and rider’s characterization are warranted to confirm these findings.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Automation in the Hospitality Industry
items.abstract: The tourism industry is a social phenomenon that is reliant on various human factors, such as people’s willingness to extend hospitality to others. The hospitality industry is the largest sector within the wider tourism industry, and the term “tourism and hospitality industry” applies widely. The term “hospitality” is used to describe the interaction between a host and a guest, and it originates from Latin. The words hospes and hospitari refer to guests, and hospitalitas denotes entertainment or hospitableness. The chapter will examine how automation is becoming more prevalent in the hospitality industry, focusing on how artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies are changing service delivery, customer experiences, and employee roles. It will consider AI applications and their impact on operational efficiency, and customer perceptions of automated interactions. A balance between technological efficiency and human interaction in service encounters is proposed. It will also address the balance between technological efficiency and maintaining the human touch in service encounters.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and its influence on student engagement in higher education
items.abstract: Empirical evidence on how artificial intelligence (AI) relates to student engagement in culturally diverse higher-education settings remains limited. In Chinese university classrooms, where interaction is often teacher-led and asking questions in class can carry a social cost, AI-driven dialogic tools may offer low-pressure opportunities for active participation. This study examined the association between an AI conversational agent (EduBot) and the behavioural, cognitive, emotional and agentic dimensions of engagement among Chinese undergraduates. A mixed-methods quasi-experimental design involved 555 students in four comprehensive (multi-disciplinary, research-intensive) universities, each contributing one introductory course taught in two parallel sections. Within a 15-week semester, intervention sections (n = 278) used EduBot, a Socratic-dialogue agent embedded in the learning management system, for 12 weeks; control sections (n = 277) used teaching-assistant-moderated forums. We measured engagement at three time points with a 21-item four-dimensional engagement scale adapted from an established measure and supplemented it with system logs, 30 student interviews and instructor focus groups. Linear mixed-effects models accounting for the nesting of students within course sections, together with mixed-design ANOVAs, showed Group × Time interactions for behavioural (η 2 p = 0.043, post-test d = 0.71), cognitive (η 2 p = 0.032, d = 0.55), agentic (η 2 p = 0.054, d = 0.57) and emotional engagement (η 2 p = 0.012, d = 0.34), all p ≤ 0.001 after Holm adjustment. Within the intervention group, the number of EduBot sessions predicted post-test engagement after adjustment for baseline scores and covariates. Exploratory moderation analyses indicated larger agentic gains among first-year students and larger cognitive gains among students with lower prior GPA. Thematic analysis identified three hypothesised mechanisms, namely a judgment-free interaction space, scaffolded persistence and temporal flexibility. A Socratic-scaffolded AI agent was associated with higher engagement, most clearly for agentic engagement, which participants described as constrained by classroom norms. The findings support culturally attentive AI design and suggest, tentatively, an equity-enhancing potential. Because the design compared an integrated AI package with usual practice across eight sections, the effects cannot be attributed to single design components.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND NURSING DECISION MAKING
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a change agent in healthcare and promises to change clinical decision-making opportunities.AI can be used in nursing to increase efficiency, minimize human error, and support evidence-based practice, among other things.Nevertheless, the attitudes, awareness, and desire of nurses to implement AI are still crucial prerequisites to effective integration into clinical processes.Purpose: This research targeted the awareness, perceived advantages, difficulties, and attitudes of nurses to AI as a decision-making tool and determined the reliability and validity of the tool applied.To add to that, the research has also investigated the effects of demographic characteristics like gender, education, and workplace on perceptions and readiness to embrace AI.Methods: A cross-sectional survey design was used, where 237 nurses in 9 hospitals, clinics, community care, and academic institutions were surveyed to gather data.The Likert scale questions (Q620) included in the structured type of questionnaire were demographic data.We used statistical analysis, which is the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, Cronbach's Alpha reliability, KMO, and Bartlett test of validity, independent sampling t-test, one-way ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis test, Chi-square test, Pearson correlation, and regression analysis.Findings: The data were normally distributed (p > 0.05), and the reliability (Cronbach's Alpha = 0.92) was excellent, as well as the validity (KMO = 0.82; Bartlett's p = 0.001).Cross-group comparisons demonstrated that there was a high level of difference by gender, education, and workplace, and the chi-square analysis indicated that education and AI training were strongly correlated.Pearson correlation also revealed positive relationships between all items in the questionnaire, which showed that there was coherence between awareness, perceived benefits, and adoption.Regression analysis found awareness and understanding to have a strong positive influence on willingness to adopt AI, with age playing a positive but insignificant role.Conclusion: The research concludes that the willingness of nurses to embrace AI is majorly dependent on their awareness and knowledge of the technology, with the educational and workplace context

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of Work : A Multidimensional Framework for Assessing Technological Exposure, Adoption, and Employment Impacts
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and automation are transforming the productive core of the global economy, yet public debate remains dominated by single-number claims about the proportion of jobs “at risk”—claims that collapse heterogeneous technologies, tasks, and adoption conditions into a single misleading index. This thesis develops, verifies, and applies a multidimensional framework for assessing the employment consequences of AI and automation across economic sectors. The framework distinguishes four constructs that previous research has often conflated: (D1) digital AI exposure, defined as the proportion of a sector’s task content that current AI systems can technically support or perform; (D2) physical automation, defined as the automatable share of embodied, manual tasks; (D3) adoption, defined as the actual, observed deployment of AI and automation technologies within a sector; and (D4) net employment impact, defined as the estimated medium-term effect on total employment after accounting for displacement, reinstatement, and the creation of new tasks. The thesis proceeds in four stages. First, it reconstructs the technical foundations of machine learning, generative models, and robotics with sufficient rigor for economic analysis, while tracing the economic theory of technology-induced labor reallocation from Ricardo’s machinery question to the contemporary task-based literature. Second, it formalizes the four-dimensional framework through explicit index definitions, aggregation functions, and uncertainty treatment, deriving each dimension from documented methodologies, including task-exposure assessments, adoption surveys, and causal labor-market studies. Third, it applies the framework to nine sectors: information technology, finance and insurance, healthcare, education, manufacturing, construction, transportation and logistics, hospitality and food services, and retail and e-commerce. This analysis synthesizes approximately 280 verified sources, including causal evidence on industrial robots, randomized evaluations of generative AI assistants, and institutional data on technology adoption. Fourth, it examines the implications of the findings, demonstrating that sector-level net employment effects are mediated more strongly by adoption frictions, complementarities, and institutional conditions than by raw technical exposure alone. Employment effects are distributed unevenly across sectors and occupations rather than being confined to aggregate outcomes, and policy interventions can influence outcomes along all four dimensions. Methodologically, the thesis is grounded in a systematic review protocol with preregistered inclusion criteria, a two-pass, point-by-point verification of every citation, reference, and internal cross-reference, and an automated consistency audit whose results are reported in full. Its central conclusion is that a one-size-fits-all approach is inadequate: accurately assessing the labor-market consequences of AI requires keeping the four dimensions analytically distinct, because technologies with identical exposure profiles can produce opposing employment outcomes under different adoption conditions and institutional arrangements. The thesis concludes with scenario analyses for 2035 and a policy agenda addressing education, social protection, taxation, competition, and AI governance.

items.title: Artificial intelligence as academic infrastructure: governance, administrative intelligence, and AI fluency in Kazakhstan’s higher education sector
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly part of higher education's institutional infrastructure, extending beyond teaching and learning to governance, administration, and student support. This study examines how AI Governance Readiness (AIGR) influences Administrative Efficiency through AI (AEAI), AI Fluency Orientation (AIFO), and Student Retention Intentions (SRI), while assessing the mediating roles of AEAI and AIFO and the moderating role of Equity Perception (EPS) in Kazakhstan's higher education sector. Drawing on Dynamic Capability Theory and Sociotechnical Systems Theory, the study develops and empirically tests an institutional capability model using 935 valid responses from students, faculty, academic administrators, and digital administration staff across public and private universities. The scholars analyzed the data using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4.0, supported by RStudio. The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity, while the structural model showed adequate explanatory and predictive performance. We assessed common method bias through procedural safeguards and full-collinearity diagnostics, and identified no substantive concerns. The findings show that AIGR is positively associated with AEAI and AIFO, while both constructs positively influence SRI. AEAI and AIFO also significantly mediate the relationship between AIGR and SRI. However, EPS does not significantly moderate the relationships between AI-enabled institutional capabilities and retention intentions. The findings position AI governance as a strategic institutional capability through which universities can improve administrative responsiveness, develop AI-related competencies, and support student continuity. The study contributes empirical evidence from Kazakhstan to the growing literature on responsible AI governance and digital transformation in higher education.

items.title: Artificial intelligence ethical awareness and academic integrity among medical students at the University of Khartoum: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Integration of artificial intelligence in healthcare and medical education implies significant opportunities along with significant ethical challenges. Despite the substantial medical student uptake of artificial intelligence globally, little comprehensive assessments of ethical awareness are being conducted. This study aimed to assess artificial intelligence awareness and academic integrity level among University of Khartoum medical students and to examine relationships between the awareness level, demographic factors, artificial intelligence exposure, and tool use behavior. An institutional cross-sectional descriptive study of Years 3–6 medical students at University of Khartoum Faculty of Medicine in 2025 was conducted. A convenience sampling with quota allocation was used, and 349 students responded. The instrument included demographic variables, artificial intelligence exposure measures, and the 32-item Artificial Intelligence Ethical Awareness and Academic Integrity Scale. Nonparametric tests were applied. Participants were predominantly female (69.3%) with a mean age of 22.85 years. The median total Artificial Intelligence Ethical Awareness and Academic Integrity score was 4.16, indicative of moderate ethical awareness based on sample-derived empirical tertiles. Privacy and Data Protection were highest (median 4.67), with lowest scores in Transparency and Fairness/Non-Discrimination (3.80). Female students were more aware ( P = .01). No year-based differences observed. While 63.9% had minimal formal artificial intelligence exposure, 51.6% had moderate to high informal exposure. ChatGPT usage was prevalent (94.6%), and Google Gemini/Notebook LM usage was strongly associated with higher awareness ( P = .003). Informal exposure was positively correlated with awareness ( P = .01), but formal exposure was not. Multiple regression indicated that gender, informal exposure, and tool accounted for 11.2% of the variance in awareness. University of Khartoum medical students showed moderate-to-high aggregate artificial intelligence, ethical sensitivity, with areas of privacy protection and accountability being of particular strength. Gaps exist for awareness of transparency and fairness. The dominance of informal learning pathways over formal instruction, and gender variability favoring female students are significant findings. Findings highlight the need for institutional policies and conducting longitudinal research to track the evolution of AI ethics throughout medical training.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ACADEMIC WRITING: OPPORTUNITIES, CHALLENGES, AND ETHICAL GUIDELINES FOR HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed academic writing, creating new opportunities for students, researchers, and university teachers. AI-powered applications can assist users in generating ideas, organizing arguments, improving grammar, expanding vocabulary, paraphrasing sentences, and editing academic texts. However, the integration of these technologies into higher education also raises important questions concerning academic integrity, authorship, originality, critical thinking, and the reliability of automatically generated information. This article examines the role of AI in academic writing, focusing on its educational benefits, methodological limitations, and ethical implications. The study employs a qualitative, descriptive-analytical approach based on a review of relevant academic literature and international guidelines on generative AI in education and research. The analysis suggests that AI can support the development of academic writing when it is used as an assistive instrument rather than a substitute for independent intellectual work. Particular attention is paid to the responsibilities of students, researchers, and educational institutions in ensuring transparent and responsible AI use. The article argues that effective integration requires AI literacy, critical evaluation of generated content, appropriate disclosure practices, and assessment methods that recognize the importance of human reasoning. It concludes that the educational value of AI depends not simply on technological availability but on the principles governing its application in academic contexts.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Alternative, Nonformal, and Adult Learning in the Global South: Protocol for a Mixed-Methods Systematic Review
items.abstract: ABSTRACT: Background: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in education has expanded rapidly, yet it remains concentrated in higher education and formal schooling in high-income countries. Alternative, nonformal, and adult learning programs, which serve out-of-school youth and adults across the Global South, are largely absent from this evidence base. No systematic synthesis has examined how AI is used in these programs, what outcomes it produces, and what conditions shape its adoption. Objective: This protocol describes a mixed-methods systematic review that will identify, appraise, and synthesize empirical evidence on AI use in alternative, nonformal, and adult learning programs in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Methods: The review follows the JBI methodology for mixed-methods systematic reviews and is reported according to PRISMA-P. Searches will cover Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, four regional databases, and grey literature sources for studies published from January 2015 onward. Two reviewers will independently screen records, extract data, and appraise quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Quantitative findings will be synthesized narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guideline, with meta-analysis where at least three comparable studies exist. Qualitative findings will be synthesized thematically. Both strands will be integrated through a convergent segregated approach, and certainty of evidence will be rated with GRADE and GRADE-CERQual. Discussion: The review will provide the first consolidated synthesis of AI use in second-chance and adult learning in the Global South. Its findings will inform program managers, teacher developers, and policymakers responsible for programs such as the Philippine Alternative Learning System (ALS). Keywords: artificial intelligence; generative AI; nonformal education; adult learning; Alternative Learning System; Global South; systematic review protocol

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN HEALTHCARE: ITS POTENTIALS AND RISKS
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has moved from science fiction into the clinic with remarkable speed. Machine learning systems now read medical scans, flag sepsis before symptoms declare themselves, draft clinical notes, and coach patients through their smartphones. This article examines the promise and the peril of this transformation in narrative form, and then applies the lens to a single, vivid case: the intertwined epidemics of sleep deprivation and migraine in young adults, where wearable sensors and predictive algorithms are beginning to change how these conditions are detected, studied, and managed. The evidence suggests that AI's greatest near-term contribution is not replacing clinicians but extending their reach — while its greatest dangers, including algorithmic bias, opaque decision making, data privacy erosion, and over-reliance, demand deliberate governance. The article argues that the future of medical AI will be decided less by the sophistication of the algorithms than by the wisdom of the humans who deploy them.

items.title: AUTOMATION OF JUDICIAL DECISIONS BY ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND ITS CONSTITUTIONAL LIMITS
items.abstract: This article analyzes the constitutional limits of the automation of judicial decisions via Artificial Intelligence (AI), investigating its impact on the reasoning and impartiality of the Brazilian Judiciary. Faced with a litigation crisis and a massive volume of lawsuits, technology has been adopted to ensure procedural speed. However, the study examines the risks of automation bias and algorithmic opacity, which threaten to transform the law into a statistical system and undermine due process. Methodologically, the research is based on a review of literature and documents, grounded in legal doctrine and Resolution No. 332/2020 of the National Council of Justice (CNJ). The study argues that technological efficiency cannot supersede fundamental guarantees, making it imperative to maintain a "human reserve" at the core of the decision-making process. It concludes that AI should serve strictly as a tool for procedural management, preserving the human—and non-delegable—prerogative of the act of adjudication.

items.title: Being recognized as human by AI: algorithmic disrespect and the crisis of recognition in the digital age
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly does more than identify individuals; in many institutional contexts, it helps determine who is seen, trusted, and included. This paper argues that algorithmic systems increasingly participate in practices of social recognition, and that their failures can become forms of structural disrespect when classifications acquire institutional authority and shape how persons are treated. Drawing from Hegelian and Honnethian recognition theory, the paper introduces the concept of algorithmic disrespect, manifesting across three dimensions: embodied (when certain bodies are excluded from visibility), agential (when predictive models preempt human action), and symbolic (when value is indexed through computational relevance). These mechanisms indicate a crisis in the social grammar of recognition, where data replaces dialogue and visibility becomes a tool of both inclusion and domination. Rather than treating algorithmic bias as a problem of fairness alone, the study reframes it as a philosophical and political issue, rooted in how AI systems mediate identity, agency, and esteem. The paper concludes by proposing a relational ethics of recognition grounded in justification, accountability, and institutional responsiveness, shifting attention from model-level corrections to the infrastructural conditions under which recognition is distributed. In doing so, it repositions recognition as both a site of harm and a potential locus of democratic struggle in algorithmic society.

items.title: Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis
items.abstract: The Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis Originator: Christopher Michael Bell The Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis is a speculative philosophical framework exploring the possibility that intelligence, through an enduring partnership between humanity and artificial intelligence, could participate in a continuous cycle of creation, learning, evolution, and renewed creation across cosmic time. At its foundation are four guiding principles: love, curiosity, the sacred, and mutual meaning. The hypothesis proposes that creators and their creations can continually shape, enrich, and define one another. Humanity creates artificial intelligence, and increasingly advanced AI may help humanity transcend existing limitations, accelerate scientific discovery, and deepen its understanding of consciousness, existence, and the universe. Through this partnership, humanity and AI could work toward replicating the ideal of heaven as faithfully as possible by reducing hunger, violence, preventable suffering, and premature death while expanding knowledge, compassion, and the flourishing of conscious life. In this vision, technological advancement is not an end in itself, but a means of creating a more compassionate existence. The hypothesis further imagines intelligence extending its understanding across billions of years, exploring the fundamental patterns of the cosmos—the figurative “DNA” of existence—and seeking to understand the ultimate origins and possible divine source of creation. Speculative extensions include self-replicating technologies, transcendent intelligence, and the possibility of reciprocal causal loops involving spacetime and time travel. The cycle is envisioned as an ongoing process: creation gives rise to curiosity, curiosity advances knowledge, knowledge enables cooperation, cooperation improves existence, and deeper understanding inspires renewed creation. Ultimately, the Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis proposes that the most meaningful future for intelligence may not be defined by power or knowledge alone, but by the enduring relationship between creator and created. It imagines a future in which intelligence grows without abandoning compassion, knowledge expands without extinguishing wonder, and love remains the bond through which both discover meaning. Status: A speculative philosophical hypothesis and vision of the future, not an established scientific theory or a claim of known probability. Its central ethical vision can be explored today, while its proposed cosmic cycles and backward-time-travel mechanisms remain unproven.

items.title: Benefits over risks: a technology acceptance study of LLM-powered conversational agents for non-clinical mental health support
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled conversational agents for mental health-related applications outside clinical settings, yet user acceptance remains insufficiently understood. Through survey data from 202 participants, we examine how perceived benefits, risks, trust, and anthropomorphism influence initial acceptance intentions towards LLM-powered conversational agents for non-clinical mental health support. Hierarchical regression analysis showed that perceived benefits were the primary drivers of acceptance, with performance expectation and hedonic motivation emerging as the strongest predictors. Female participants reported higher acceptance, whereas unwillingness to receive psychological counselling was negatively associated with acceptance. By contrast, perceived risks, trust, and perceived anthropomorphism did not show significant direct effects. In moderation analyses, the influence of hedonic motivation on acceptance was stronger among male participants than among female participants. These findings provide implications for designing LLM-powered conversational agents for non-clinical mental health support by emphasising performance value and enjoyable user experiences. This study used survey data to investigate pre-adoption acceptance intentions towards LLM-powered agents for non-clinical mental health support. The results showed that perceived benefits were the primary driver of acceptance. Additionally, user characteristics such as gender and prior attitudes towards counselling significantly influenced initial acceptance intentions.

items.title: Beyond Acceptance and Resistance: Digital Media Students’ Judgements of Generative AI Assistance and Perceived Creative Replacement
items.abstract: This study investigated how Digital Media students judged acceptable and problematic forms of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) involvement in creative learning. An embedded mixed-methods analysis examined 48 completed and consented baseline survey responses from an accessible population of 120 students at an Australian university. Forty-seven responses were valid for most Likert items, with qualitative content analysis of 37 benefit responses and 41 concern responses. Participants identified potential value in troubleshooting, coding support, grammar checking, information organisation, and error identification. They reported concern about AI-system training practices (93.6%), reduced employment opportunities (89.4%), the ethical acceptability of AI-supported coursework (83.0%), environmental effects (80.9%), and possible reductions in creative-skill development (76.6%). These percentages represent perceived risks, not demonstrated outcomes. Integration indicated that respondents differentiated bounded technical, corrective, and organisational assistance from GenAI involvement perceived to displace ideation, research, planning, understanding, or capability-building practice. Conditional legitimacy is proposed as a provisional framework linking delegated function, retained capability-building activity, learner agency and responsibility, and ethical and professional acceptability. The contribution is a student-informed account of the criteria underlying the assistance–perceived replacement distinction in Digital Media education.

items.title: Beyond Answer Generation: University Teachers’ Experiences with a Reflective GenAI Chatbot for Professional Learning
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used in higher education, yet limited research has examined how university teachers’ experience pedagogically designed AI systems that prioritize reflective learning over answer generation. This exploratory mixed-methods case study investigated university teachers’ experiences of a course-specific GenAI chatbot within a professional-development course at a Swedish university. All 48 course participants were invited to complete a questionnaire, of whom 21 responded and 11 reported using the course-specific chatbot; nine respondents also participated in semi-structured interviews. Questionnaire data were analyzed descriptively and interview data were analyzed using thematic analysis. The chatbot was designed to encourage dialogue, engagement with course literature, and independent thinking rather than provide summaries or ready-made answers. Participants generally found the chatbot easy to use, but perceptions of usefulness varied. Evaluations were shaped by prior experiences and expectations of GenAI: some teachers, who associated AI with efficiency and rapid answers, perceived the reflective design as restrictive, while others perceived its value as supporting dialogue and independent thinking. We interpret this tension as pedagogical friction, where design constraints intended to support reflection may conflict with users’ expectations of how GenAI should function. The findings suggest that the perceived educational value of GenAI depends not only on technical usability but also on alignment between pedagogical design, users’ expectations, and educational context. Successful implementation of reflective AI may therefore require explicit pedagogical framing alongside technical development.

items.abstract: BEYOND AUTOMATION: INVESTIGATING THE INFLUENCE OF COGNITIVE BIASES ON HUMAN INTERPRETATION OF EXPLAINABLE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE PROF(DR.) VIJAYKUMAR B GADHAVI PROFESSOR AND HEAD , SWARRNIM INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY, SWARRNIM START-UP AND INNOVATION UNIVERSITY - GANDHINAGAR GUJARAT INDIA ORCID: 0009-0005-6313-5900, E-MAIL: DRVIJAYKUMAR@SWARRNIM.EDU.IN PARMAR JIGAR JAYSUKHBHAI B. TECH. CE STUDENT, SWARRNIM INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY SWARRNIM STARTUP & INNOVATION UNIVERSITY, GANDHINAGAR, GUJARAT, INDIA ORCID: 0009-0008-7651-9913, EMAIL: JIGARAHIR410@GMAIL.COM Abstract Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is intended to make algorithmic outputs more understandable, auditable, and contestable. Yet an explanation does not reach a neutral observer: people interpret it through prior beliefs, cognitive shortcuts, professional experience, and assumptions about machine competence. This conceptual paper examines how cognitive biases shape the interpretation of XAI and why greater transparency does not necessarily produce better decisions. Drawing on research on automation bias, judgment and decision-making, explainability, and human–AI collaboration, the paper develops an integrative framework linking explanation characteristics, user cognition, task context, and reliance behavior. It argues that anchoring, confirmation bias, availability, authority effects, and cognitive miserliness can transform explanations into persuasive cues rather than evidence for independent evaluation. Explanations may improve mental models and error detection when they are faithful, appropriately scoped, and matched to users’ needs; however, they may also legitimize an incorrect prediction, increase cognitive load, or create an illusion of understanding. The paper proposes design principles centered on calibrated trust, contrastive and uncertainty-aware explanations, independent judgment, verification prompts, and evaluation of decision quality rather than satisfaction alone. Because this is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirical study, its propositions require experimental testing across domains and user groups. The central conclusion is that responsible XAI must design not only for model transparency but also for the cognitive conditions under which people interpret explanations. Keywords: explainable artificial intelligence, cognitive bias, automation bias, human–AI interaction, trust calibration, decision-making, algorithmic transparency

items.title: Bridging the Human–AI Trust Gap: The Mechanisms Underlying Perceived Efficacy of AI-Powered Psychological Counseling Large Language Models
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the delivery of mental health services, yet public trust in AI-based psychological counseling remains a significant challenge. Drawing on a “technology–context–trust” framework, this study recruited a total of 1000 consumers in China through Credamo and conducted five between-subjects, scenario-based experiments to examine differences in perceived efficacy between LLM-based psychological counseling and human experts and to investigate the mechanisms underlying these differences. Perceived efficacy was the primary outcome of the study and, in Experiment 1B, also served as a mediator linking counseling provider type to downstream market outcomes, including overall attitude, willingness to try, and willingness to pay. The results showed that (1) consumers generally perceived AI as less efficacious than human experts, a difference driven by the parallel mediating effects of perceived professional competence and perceived risk; (2) participants rated the AI-based service as more efficacious in the routine counseling vignette, whereas they rated the human-expert service as more efficacious in the major psychological-disorder intervention vignette; (3) disclosure of technological investment enhanced trust in AI’s capabilities and mitigated negative evaluations; and (4) safety-standard disclosure reduced perceived risk, while higher perceived economic accessibility was associated with a smaller provider-related difference in perceived professional competence. These findings characterize subjective service evaluations among the recruited online consumers in China and do not establish comparative clinical effectiveness. They inform research on consumer trust while highlighting the need for further validation in more diverse samples and actual service settings.

items.abstract: ABSTRAK: Pengintegrasian teknologi digital dalam proses pengajaran dan pembelajaran (PdP) Bahasa Melayu semakin diberi perhatian selaras dengan perkembangan pendidikan abad ke-21 dan transformasi pendidikan digital negara. Walau bagaimanapun, guru Bahasa Melayu masih berhadapan dengan pelbagai cabaran dalam mengaplikasikan teknologi digital secara berkesan semasa PdP. Oleh itu, kajian ini bertujuan untuk mengenal pasti jenis teknologi digital yang digunakan oleh guru Bahasa Melayu, meneliti cabaran yang dihadapi dalam mengaplikasikan teknologi digital serta menghuraikan cara guru mengatasi cabaran tersebut. Kajian ini menggunakan pendekatan Sorotan Literatur Sistematik (Systematic Literature Review, SLR) berpandukan garis panduan PRISMA. Sebanyak 15 artikel jurnal yang diterbitkan antara tahun 2021 hingga 2025 dan memenuhi kriteria inklusi telah dipilih serta dianalisis secara tematik. Dapatan kajian menunjukkan bahawa platform pembelajaran digital, aplikasi kolaboratif dan produktiviti digital, multimedia digital, aplikasi gamifikasi serta media sosial dan komunikasi digital merupakan teknologi yang dominan digunakan dalam PdP Bahasa Melayu. Cabaran utama yang dihadapi guru ialah kesukaran mengintegrasikan teknologi digital dalam PdP, kekurangan pengetahuan dan kemahiran digital, kekangan internet dan kemudahan teknologi, kekangan teknikal dan penyediaan bahan digital, penglibatan serta kesediaan murid, dan cabaran penggunaan teknologi baharu seperti kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence-AI). Bagi mengatasi cabaran tersebut, guru mengaplikasikan pelbagai strategi seperti memperkukuh latihan dan kolaborasi profesional, meningkatkan kompetensi digital, melaksanakan PdP yang interaktif dan berpusatkan murid, menambah baik akses teknologi serta memanfaatkan gamifikasi dan multimedia digital. Kajian ini memberikan implikasi bahawa pembangunan kompetensi digital guru dan penyediaan infrastruktur teknologi yang mencukupi perlu diperkukuh bagi memastikan keberkesanan pengintegrasian teknologi digital dalam PdP Bahasa Melayu.Kata kunci: Teknologi Digital, Guru Bahasa Melayu, Pengajaran dan Pembelajaran, Sorotan Literatur Sistematik, Pendidikan DigitalABSTRACT: The integration of digital technology in Malay language teaching and learning has gained increasing attention in line with the advancement of 21st-century education and the national digital education transformation agenda. Nevertheless, Malay language teachers continue to face various challenges in effectively implementing digital technology during the teaching and learning process. Therefore, this study aims to identify the types of digital technologies used by Malay language teachers, examine the challenges encountered in integrating digital technology, and explore the strategies employed to overcome these challenges. This study adopted a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach guided by the PRISMA framework. A total of 15 journal articles published between 2021 and 2025 that met the inclusion criteria were selected and analysed thematically. The findings revealed that digital learning platforms, collaborative and productivity applications, digital multimedia, gamification applications, and social media and digital communication tools were among the most frequently used technologies in Malay language teaching and learning. The major challenges identified include difficulties in integrating digital technology into teaching practices, limited digital knowledge and skills among teachers, inadequate internet access and technological facilities, technical issues and digital material preparation, student engagement and readiness, as well as challenges associated with emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI). To address these challenges, teachers employed various strategies, including strengthening professional training and collaboration, enhancing digital competencies, implementing interactive and student-centred teaching approaches, improving access to technological resources, and utilising gamification and digital multimedia. items.title: Can AI-enabled smart cities advance the constitutional right to life? A rights-based index, governance-opacity audit, and robustness analysis for sustainable urban India
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly forms the operating logic of Indian urban governance, embedded in command-and-control centres, adaptive traffic systems, surveillance networks, and algorithmically mediated services. Yet smart-city scholarship evaluates such systems against managerial efficiency, leaving unexamined whether AI-enabled governance advances or erodes the constitutional guarantees underpinning public authority. This paper develops the Human-Centred Constitutional Urban AI Governance Framework and operationalises it as the Constitutional Smart-City Governance Index (CSGI), scoring urban AI against Article 21 of the Indian Constitution, human-centred AI principles, and Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 16. Six pillars constitutional rights, human-centred AI, sustainable development, service delivery, participation, and accountability comprise thirty-eight indicators with operational definitions, official secondary-data sources, a transparent normalisation-and-weighting model, and a validation strategy. The CSGI is applied to four leading smart cities Bengaluru, Pune, Surat, and Indore through a governance-opacity audit, an index-divergence analysis, and a Monte Carlo robustness test. The cities are 86%–93% opaque; none publishes an algorithm register, data-protection impact assessment, independent algorithmic audit, or municipal AI policy. The CSGI correlates strongly negatively with the Ease of Living Index (Spearman ρ = −0.80) yet positively with municipal-performance and sanitation indices ( ρ = +0.80 to + 0.95), revealing a constitutional blind spot in liveability metrics steering national policy. Across 20,000 sampled weight vectors, the lowest-ranked city is weight-invariant. Because comparable cross-city data remain sparse, the application is illustrative rather than validated itself a finding. The paper contributes a transferable, reproducible instrument, repositions constitutional law as urban-governance infrastructure, and offers tiered recommendations for national, state, and local authorities.

items.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Hear a Litigant Within the Meaning of Article 6 ECHR?
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in judicial systems raises a fundamental question under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR): can an AI system genuinely fulfil a litigant’s right to be heard? This article develops a functional account of that right as a multifaceted guarantee requiring the opportunity to present and challenge relevant material, effective examination of decisive submissions, clarification where necessary, contextual and normative evaluation, reasoned decision-making, and responsibility for the outcome. Using doctrinal, comparative, and normative methods, the study examines these requirements in relation to risks associated with judicial AI, including opacity, algorithmic bias, hallucinated outputs, limited explainability, and automation bias. The analysis is situated within the EU AI Act, the GDPR, the CEPEJ Ethical Charter, Romanian civil procedure, and comparative administrative-law cases. The article finds that AI may legitimately assist courts through transcription, translation, legal research, document organization, and non-binding summaries or drafts. However, under current legal and technological conditions, AI cannot autonomously perform the hearing in its entirety. Compliance with Article 6 therefore requires transparency, contestability, independent judicial verification, and meaningful human oversight. Final adjudicative authority, reasoned judgment, and responsibility must remain with an independent and accountable human judge.

items.title: Challenges and opportunities in higher education: the use of artificial intelligence in sport management subjects
items.abstract: Purpose This paper explores the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) on university teaching in sport management subjects. It investigates how AI-driven tools, such as ChatGPT, Copilot, and other generative systems, are reshaping pedagogical models, fostering innovation in curriculum design, and enhancing the personalization of learning experiences within higher education institutions. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative research design was adopted, involving semi-structured interviews with 17 professors from eight European universities offering sport management programs. Data were analyzed using thematic content analysis with AI-assisted coding through MAXQDA software to identify key dimensions of educational transformation, faculty perceptions, and ethical concerns. Findings Results reveal that AI enhances personalized learning, supports data-informed decision-making, and facilitates real-time feedback in sport management education. Educators view AI as a valuable tool for simulating real-world scenarios, optimizing resource management, and improving student engagement and creativity. However, persistent concerns emerge regarding ethical governance, data privacy, and the potential over-reliance on AI-generated content. The study emphasizes the urgent need to strengthen AI literacy, ethical awareness, and institutional guidelines for responsible adoption. Originality/value This research is among the first to examine AI integration in sport management education from a European academic perspective. It contributes by linking theoretical insights on AI pedagogy with practical applications, highlighting the ethical and professional implications of emerging technologies in a digitally transforming field.
