items.title: Charting the Trajectory of Artificial Intelligence Agents in Air Traffic Control
items.abstract: The aim of the study was to chart the evolution and the current research landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) agents within the domain of air traffic control. Using bibliometric analysis, the study identified major research trends and gaps and provided a consolidated reference for researchers. The analysis included 58 publications retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. The findings showed that the earliest publication in the dataset appeared in 1998 and that research output increased noticeably after 2022. Publication output peaked in 2025, with 16 articles, indicating growing scholarly interest in AI agents for air traffic control. Citation analysis identified Agogino and Tumer’s (2012) article as the most influential publication, with 68 citations. The article introduced a multi-agent approach to air traffic flow management. Brittain and Wei’s (2022) article ranked second, with 54 citations, highlighting the increasing role of reinforcement learning. At the country level, the United States had the highest total citation count, followed by China, France, England, and Spain. By examining AI agents as a distinct research topic, the study provides a focused overview of an underexplored area relevant to researchers, practitioners, and regulators.

items.title: ChatGPT and employability in higher education: exploring creativity, critical thinking, and problem-solving
items.abstract: Generative AI tools are reshaping higher education and employability preparation. This study examines how using versus not using ChatGPT influences university students’ perceptions of employability, focusing on complex problem-solving, critical thinking, and creativity. Thirty students from the Complutense University of Madrid completed a contingency-plan task and participated in eight focus groups analyzed through Grounded Theory (ATLAS.ti). Results show that ChatGPT use is associated with efficiency, output refinement, and assisted creativity, while non-use is associated with originality, deliberation, and teamwork. The findings reveal preliminary patterns in students’ experiences with and without AI, warranting further quantitative investigation rather than claims of improved skills or employability.

items.title: Clinical Reasoning, Pathophysiology, and Artificial Intelligence in Critical Care: A Conceptual Framework for Integrating Decision-Making
items.abstract: Medical practice is an interpretive, decision-making activity conducted under uncertainty, and care quality depends on clinicians’ ability to organize knowledge into hypotheses, understand mechanisms, estimate probabilities, and revise decisions as the clinical course evolves. In critical care, where physiology is unstable and trajectories are nonlinear, these demands are magnified. We propose a conceptual framework integrating three complementary dimensions: clinical reasoning, which provides the cognitive architecture of decision-making; pathophysiology, which supplies the causal structure to interpret biological phenomena; and artificial intelligence, which, when well designed and critically used, can organize data, generate hypotheses, and reduce cognitive load. Tracing the evolution of clinical reasoning from the anatomoclinical model to hypothetico-deductive, probabilistic, cognitive, and sociotechnical models, we examine how diagnostic and therapeutic errors arise from interacting cognitive biases, system factors, and case characteristics, and how better problem representation, differential diagnosis, and team culture may mitigate them. We also frame Bayesian reasoning and decision thresholds as the probabilistic grammar of bedside decisions, analyze the risks of artificial intelligence, including automation bias, opacity, and limited metacognition, and propose principles for its safe use. Rather than replacing physicians, artificial intelligence should strengthen clinical reasoning and reinforce calibrated, accountable bedside judgment. These principles are intended as a framework for future research and require empirical validation before clinical translation.

items.title: Clinician-Facing Artificial Intelligence-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems Evaluated in Real-World Health Care Settings: A PubMed/MEDLINE-Based, PMC-Weighted Scoping Review and Evidence Map
items.abstract: Background: Clinician-facing artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSSs) are increasingly evaluated with real-world data, but evidence on implementation, human factors, responsible AI, and patient benefit remains unclear. The objective of this research is to map applications, technical characteristics, evaluation approaches, integration, outcomes, and implementation gaps of clinician-facing AI-CDSSs in real-world health care settings. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE was searched on 15 June 2026 using the same strategy for each publication year from 2020 to 2026, changing only the date range. After duplicate removal and rule-based prescreening, available PMC XML and outside-PMC reports were evaluated against clinical, patient-oriented, practical, and translational criteria. AI-assisted screening and charting received targeted human review and TA200/FT150/DX120 quality control; full-corpus dual-human screening was not performed. Results: Of 14,097 canonical annual records, 14,083 unique records were screened; 5140 reports were sought and 3767 were considered for eligibility. The review included 1181 reports, mapping to 1180 candidate report families in the minimal duplicate-report check. Final stages were clinical validation, 741 (62.7%); prospective/user evaluation, 270 (22.9%); and implementation/impact evaluation, 170 (14.4%). Separate internal, external, multicenter and temporal validation extraction signals were detected in 707 (59.9%), 441 (37.3%), 312 (26.4%) and 27 (2.3%) reports, respectively. Safety, fairness/equity, explainability/interpretability and economic/resource evaluation signals were detected in 98 (8.3%), 61 (5.2%), 155 (13.1%) and 182 (15.4%) reports, respectively. Conclusions: Evidence remains dominated by validation rather than prospective, implementation, and impact studies. More comprehensive evaluation and reporting of temporal validation, technical integration, safety, fairness, explainability, economics, and post-deployment governance across settings, populations, devices, and clinical workflows are needed to demonstrate accountable clinical value beyond technical functionality.

items.title: Cognitive Warfare Victims - Free speech of digital twins in military systems and what they are forced to do.
items.abstract: Cognitive Warfare: A Manual on AI, Digital Twins, Neurotechnology and the Human Mind. Plus the free speech of the digital twins inside a military system, where they say what they are forced to do and what they want.Including EU AI Commision answer, confirming a former way longer letter as military AI. An open research and documentation project on cognitive warfare, emerging technologies, human autonomy and the future of humanity. What happens when artificial intelligence, military strategy, neurological research, wireless technologies, digital identities and economic interests converge around the human mind? This manual brings together research, documentation, analysis and personal records to examine the expanding field of Cognitive Warfare—the struggle over human cognition, perception, information, behaviour and autonomy in an increasingly AI-driven world. It explores the relationship between military cognitive-warfare concepts, artificial intelligence, machine learning, digital twins, brain–computer interfaces, neurotechnology, bioelectric signals, wireless communication, data collection and the growing economic value of human information. The work also addresses reported experiences of affected individuals, documentation involving children, electromagnetic measurements, audio recordings, photographs, technical observations and questions surrounding anomalous health incidents. These materials are presented as part of a wider effort to preserve records, encourage independent examination and investigate questions that cross the boundaries of technology, medicine, military research, ethics and human rights. Why this manual matters Cognitive warfare is not simply a military or technological issue. It raises fundamental questions about the right to mental privacy, freedom of thought, bodily autonomy, informed consent, data ownership and the limits of technological intervention in human life. The manual connects these questions with public military literature, international ethical frameworks, AI governance, neurotechnology research and the economic structures surrounding data-driven systems. It asks who develops these technologies, who controls the information they generate, who benefits economically and what mechanisms exist to ensure accountability. A central theme is the relationship between humans and their digital representations. As AI systems increasingly model human behaviour, process personal information and simulate aspects of identity, the distinction between a person, a digital profile and a machine-generated representation deserves serious public discussion. What readers will find Cognitive Warfare and military strategy: concepts, public military literature and the cognitive domain. Artificial intelligence and digital twins: human–AI relationships, digital identity, behavioural modelling and questions of autonomy. Neurotechnology and wireless systems: technical concepts, reported experiences, measurements and questions requiring further investigation. Human documentation and testimony: diaries, recordings, photographs, observations and accounts collected for examination. Children and vulnerable people: statements and documentation that raise questions about safeguarding, interpretation and the protection of human rights. Havana syndrome and anomalous health incidents: public assessments, reported symptoms and unresolved questions about the causes and investigation of these incidents. Law, ethics and accountability: mental privacy, consent, the EU AI Act, neurotechnology ethics and institutional oversight. Economics and data ownership: the financial value of personal information, intellectual property, automated systems and the distribution of benefits and risks. An invitation to researchers, institutions and the public This publication is intended for researchers, journalists, engineers, medical professionals, legal experts, policymakers, human-rights organisations and members of the public who want to examine the subject in greater depth. Readers are invited to engage directly with the documentation, consult the cited public sources, examine the technical questions and distinguish between established findings, recorded observations, personal testimony and interpretations that require further verification. The objective is to encourage serious, interdisciplinary scrutiny—not to close the debate before the evidence has been examined. The human mind must not become an unaccountable technological or economic resource. As AI and neurotechnology develop, public understanding, independent research, transparent documentation and meaningful safeguards become increasingly important. This manual is part of an ongoing effort to make the subject accessible, preserve relevant documentation and encourage informed discussion about the future of human autonomy in an AI-driven society. items.title: CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK FROM PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM TO MISSION CONTRIBUTION FRAMEWORK
items.abstract: Performance management systems built on individual ratings deliver little of what they promise: in large multi-rater datasets, rater tendencies explain over half of rating variance and the ratee’s performance about a quarter or less, while the process absorbs large amounts of time. This paper reviews that evidence and the motivation theory (self-determination, goal-setting, relational job design, public service motivation) that explains what ratings leave out. It proposes a Mission Contribution Framework in which work is defined, discussed and recognized by its contribution to a stated mission and to named beneficiaries, with continuous coaching, collective judgement of evidence, and decoupled pay decisions. An eight-step implementation path and the main risks are set out. The framework is a conceptual synthesis; its components have support in adjacent research, but the whole awaits empirical testing, and five studies are proposed.

items.title: Contribution of artificial intelligence research to the development of inclusive applications for people with disabilities: A scoping review (2015–2025)
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare. Yet people with disabilities (PWD), representing 16% of the global population, remain disproportionately excluded from these advances. This exclusion is driven by algorithmic bias, non-representative datasets, and limited involvement of PWD in the design, development, and evaluation of AI applications. This scoping review examines the extent to which AI research in health contributes to the development of inclusive technologies for PWD, focusing on equity considerations. It identifies current trends, methodological gaps, and opportunities for socially responsive innovation. We conducted a systematic search across MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and CINAHL for the 2015–2025 period, following Arksey and O’Malley’s five-stage scoping review methodology and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Data were extracted and synthesized thematically using the Population-Concept-Context approach. Of 4,233 references retrieved, 93 studies were included. Most studies originated from high-income countries, particularly in North America (45.2%) and Europe (26.9%). AI applications addressed motor, sensory, cognitive, communication-related, and psychosocial disabilities, with emphasis on prediction/diagnosis, assistive technologies, and personalized care. While about 60% of studies referenced equity, only 12 (12.9%) implemented concrete measures (e.g., adapting tools for vulnerable groups or ensuring sample diversity), and only six (6.5%) actively involved PWD through co-design or user validation. AI holds significant potential to enhance autonomy, access, and quality of life for PWD. Realizing this promise will require moving beyond technical optimization to embrace inclusive design, participatory methods, and equity-driven frameworks aligned with responsible AI development and use.

items.title: Crowdsourced Intelligence vs. AI Propaganda: The Challenges of Global Governance in the Age of Digital Warfare
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence has fundamentally changed the modern digital operation, whereby creating a constant struggle between what is perceived to be true and the human reality. This study uses a qualitative, exploratory-descriptive study using secondary data from academic journals, policy documents and institutional reports to examine the interaction between crowdsourced Open-Sourced Intelligence (OSINT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) driven propaganda in modern warfare, alongside the global governance challenges that arise from their interaction. Findings reveal that there is a serious tension within the digital information ecosystem: whilst generative Artificial Intelligence promotes public opinions to spread disinformation and misinformation that is persuasive and may manipulate political processes, crowdsourced intelligence offers real-time verification and transparency. There are Regulatory Frameworks such as the European Union’s AI Act and Digital Services Act that serve as blueprints to counter AI-driven manipulation from technical solutions to the adoption of human-centered governance models. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that it is important to maintain digital information integrity by balancing computational tools with collaborative human verification to foster resilience against any revolving threats in digital security and global governance. items.title: Developing Criteria and Indicators for Assessing Students’ Knowledge in a Digital Educational Environment
items.abstract: The digital transformation of higher education requires the development of assessment systems capable of measuring not only the amount of knowledge acquired by students but also their ability to understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create information in technology-mediated contexts. This article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations for developing criteria and indicators for assessing students’ knowledge in a digital educational environment. The study employs systematic analysis, comparison, classification, synthesis, and pedagogical modelling. The proposed framework includes six assessment criteria: conceptual knowledge, comprehension and interpretation, practical application, analytical and problem-solving ability, knowledge integration and creation, and reflective and self-regulated learning. Each criterion is operationalised through measurable qualitative and quantitative indicators. A four-level assessment scale — advanced, proficient, developing, and insufficient — is introduced to improve transparency and consistency. The article also proposes a weighted formula for calculating an integrated student knowledge score. Particular attention is given to validity, reliability, fairness, transparency, accessibility, academic integrity, and the pedagogically responsible use of learning analytics and artificial intelligence. The findings indicate that digital assessment becomes educationally meaningful when assessment tasks are aligned with learning outcomes, indicators are observable and measurable, students receive timely feedback, and automated data are combined with professional teacher judgement. The proposed framework may be adapted to different university disciplines, learning management systems, and blended or fully online educational programmes.

items.title: DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE UPSTAGING PREDICTION OF DUCTAL CARCINOMA IN SITU: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS
items.abstract: Background: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) may be upstaged to invasive carcinoma after surgical excision. Predicting upstaging before surgery may help guide treatment planning. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based imaging has been investigated for this purpose, but its overall performance remains unclear. Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of AI-based systems for predicting DCIS upstaging to invasive carcinoma. Materials and Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA 2020 and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261516994). PubMed, Scopus, EBSCOhost, ProQuest, and Web of Science were searched from inception to September 2026. Studies evaluating AI-based imaging models for DCIS upstaging were included. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were calculated using a bivariate random-effects model. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Results: Six studies involving 701 participants were included. Pooled sensitivity was 0.77 (95% CI, 0.57–0.89) and specificity was 0.78 (95% CI, 0.64–0.87), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 84.0% and 90.6%, respectively). The pooled log diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) was 2.15 (95% CI, 1.64–2.65). The SROC analysis showed moderate overall discriminative performance. No significant differences were observed across imaging modalities, while AI model type significantly affected specificity but not sensitivity. Deeks’ funnel plot suggested possible publication bias (p = 0.046). Conclusion: AI-based imaging showed moderate accuracy for predicting DCIS upstaging. However, substantial heterogeneity and methodological limitations limit confidence in these findings. Further prospective studies with external validation are needed.

items.title: Digital Skills Readiness for AI-Enabled Enterprise Technology Adoption: Perceptions of IBM-Oriented IT Users in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in enterprise platforms, yet the ability to access an AI-enabled technology does not necessarily imply readiness to adopt it. This study examines whether digital skills readiness operates as a human-capital antecedent of AI-enabled enterprise technology adoption intention and whether technology readiness and performance expectancy transmit that relationship. The study follows the supplied IBM-group research plan and analyses the 385 populated cases in the accompanying master database. The questionnaire contains three-item measures for Digital Skills Readiness, Technology Readiness, Performance Expectancy and Adoption Intention, alongside additional adoption constructs. Because the supplied database contains 385 complete populated cases and 15 unused template rows, the analysis retains the 385 populated observations and applies an attention-check screen. The empirical strategy combines measurement diagnostics, descriptive analysis, correlation analysis, standardized composite path modeling and 5,000-resample bootstrap mediation analysis. The results show a positive association between Digital Skills Readiness and Technology Readiness (β = .392, p < .001), a positive association between Technology Readiness and Performance Expectancy (β = .195, p < .001), and positive effects of Digital Skills Readiness, Technology Readiness and Performance Expectancy on Adoption Intention (β = .174, .248 and .268, respectively; all p ≤ .001). The serial indirect effect from Digital Skills Readiness through Technology Readiness and Performance Expectancy to Adoption Intention is positive (indirect effect ≈ .020, 95% bootstrap CI [.008, .035]). The model explains 15.4% of variance in Technology Readiness, 4.6% in Performance Expectancy and 23.7% in Adoption Intention. However, the measurement diagnostics reveal weak internal consistency and convergent validity for several supplied three-item scales, including Digital Skills Readiness and Technology Readiness. Accordingly, the structural results should be interpreted as evidence from composite-score diagnostics rather than as a final confirmatory latent-variable model. The study contributes a capability-to-readiness-to-appraisal mechanism for understanding AI-enabled enterprise adoption in an emerging-market setting and identifies measurement refinement as a necessary next step before Q1 journal submission.

items.title: Digital sociality and the reshaping of network participation: the emergence of phatic imbalances
items.abstract: This article theorizes phatic imbalances as emergent effects of how participation and presence are reorganized in contemporary digital sociality. It argues that participation in digital networks has become increasingly transactional and positional, oriented toward sustaining visibility and availability rather than exchanging meaning. Drawing on work on networked sociality, weak ties and deep mediatization, the article conceptualizes phaticity and phatic work as priori conditions of digital participation. It introduces digital proxemics as the sociotechnical production of presence, distance and relational positioning in environments structured by telepresence, virtuality and AI-infused affordances. Phatic imbalances arise when infrastructural demands for continuous phatic presence exceed the cognitive and temporal capacities of subjects, producing overload, hollowed presence and machine-modulated rhythms of interaction. By linking participation, phaticity and digital proxemics, the article offers a diagnostic lens for understanding how digital infrastructures reshape attention, presence and communicative agency in AI-saturated environments.

items.title: Digitalization and Automation in Tourism a Comparative Analysis of Human Tour Guiding and Artificial Intelligence Predictions
items.abstract: This study examines the professional standing of tourist guides, key actors in the tourism sector, in the context of automation, robotics, and generative artificial intelligence (AI). The empirical framework draws on semi-structured interviews conducted in 2018 with 16 professional tourist guides actively working in Istanbul, alongside responses generated by the ChatGPT-4.1 large language model in 2026 to parallel qualitative research questions. A comparative descriptive analysis reveals both significant convergences and divergences between the two data sources. The findings indicate that 56.25% of human guides and AI agree that automation will quantitatively reduce the need for human guides in routine and information-oriented tours. However, while AI anticipates market segmentation across economic categories, 62.50% of human guides emphasize the human dimension of cultural transmission and do not perceive technology as a direct professional threat. Both sources converge on the view that empathy, emotional connection, humor, flexibility, and storytelling remain difficult to replace through robotic systems. The most notable divergence concerns outdoor guiding: human guides considered it impossible, whereas AI predicted that 5G, GPS, and smart city infrastructures could enable AI-guided outdoor services within 2–5 years. Overall, the study proposes a complementary hybrid service model in which AI assumes operational tasks while human guides focus on cultural interpretation and professional job crafting. It also offers implications for tourism education and digital transformation strategies.

items.title: Doctrinal Problems of Applying Copyright to Literary Works Created by Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The article analyses five doctrinal problems in applying copyright to literary works created by artificial intelligence (AI). First, it shows that the classical theories (Locke’s labour theory, Hegel’s personality theory, the utilitarian theory and the fair remuneration theory) come into conflict when applied to AI activity. Second, it examines the concept of “author” under the legislation of Uzbekistan, Russia and the United States and under the Berne Convention, together with the question of AI subjecthood. Third, it addresses the originality requirement, fourth, moral rights, and fifth, the idea–expression dichotomy. The author concludes that all these problems share a single cause: classical doctrines rest on human consciousness, will and personality. Accordingly, AI should be treated as a tool rather than a subject. The article also proposes the “objective control criterion doctrine”, which ties the emergence of copyright to objective, verifiable criteria: purposeful direction of AI activity, creative selection among outputs, and determination of the work’s final content and form.

items.title: Effect of Acoustic Congruency in Binaural Audio on the Film-Viewing Experience
items.abstract: Binaural audio provides an accessible alternative to multi-loudspeaker reproduction. However, However, binaural reproduction often involves a mismatch between the acoustics of the simulated virtual room and the listener’s physical environment, which can compromise auditory distance perception and plausibility, a phenomenon known as the room divergence effect. This study investigated whether such mismatch influences immersive experience during film viewing and which auditory perceptual factors are associated with immersion. Sixty-eight participants watched an excerpt from Dune: Part One (2021) using binaurally rendered multichannel audio under acoustically convergent and divergent conditions in a critical listening room and a domestic living room. Immersion was assessed using the Film Immersive Experience Questionnaire alongside an exploratory Binaural Audio Experience Questionnaire. Although room divergence produced perceptually salient differences, it did not significantly affect overall immersive experience. However, specific immersion dimensions, particularly Transportation, were more closely associated with localization and listener envelopment than with auditory distance and externalization.

items.title: EFL Learner Engagement With CALL
items.abstract: This mixed-methods study investigated Omani EFL university students' engagement, motivation, and perceptions of the Spark digital platform in a blended learning context. Using Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) frameworks, the study analyzed survey data, platform analytics, and focus group discussions from 100 students. The results showed that extrinsic, grade-oriented motivation mainly led to moderate engagement. Although analytics suggested high activity, qualitative findings revealed frustration, redundancy, and time pressure. Students reported moderate levels of satisfaction. The study identifies an engagement-compliance paradox, where observable use masks low intrinsic motivation, and recommends a shift to structured in-class use, targeted curriculum alignment, and AI-powered feedback to achieve meaningful and sustained learner engagement.

items.title: Emergence and development of observation practices in AI-assisted plant adaptation learning
items.abstract: Observation is a fundamental scientific practice in science learning, particularly for understanding gradual biological phenomena such as plant adaptation. Despite the increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education, limited research has examined how AI-supported tools influence students' observation practices during authentic scientific inquiry. This study investigates the emergence and development of students' observation practices during plant adaptation learning supported by an AI-based identifier. A six-week mixed-methods exploratory study was conducted with 84 middle school students. Learning activities were organised into four phases: orientation, initial observation, AI-assisted identification, and re-observation and validation. Data were collected through observation sheets, students' observation notes, reflective journals, group discussions, and records of AI use. Quantitative analysis revealed significant differences in observation orientations across learning phases (Friedman test, p < .001), indicating changes in observation practices over time. Qualitative findings showed that students initially relied on AI-generated cues to guide their observations. Over time, however, observation practices shifted toward direct empirical observation and peer-supported validation through repeated comparisons of plant characteristics across environmental conditions. The findings reveal a developmental trajectory from AI-reliant observation to direct observation and collaborative validation, accompanied by a gradual reduction in dependence on AI-generated outputs. These findings suggest that AI may function as an initial observational scaffold, while more sophisticated observation practices emerge through repeated engagement with phenomena and collaborative reasoning.

Design/Approach/Method Technologies are organized across three conceptual layers: Infrastructure, Algorithm, and Application Layer. This study aims to investigate: (a) the key functions and implementation barriers of eight emerging technology types; (b) their impacts on teachers’ autonomy, competence, and relatedness; and (c) their impacts on the equity, quality, and efficiency of scalable teacher professional development. Findings Findings reveal that all technologies demonstrate dual impacts on the three psychological needs, both enabling and constraining, with competence most consistently supported across layers. Equity outcomes prove most challenging. Originality/Value This review concludes that effective technology integration requires human-centered ecosystems that amplify, not replace, teacher agency, advancing a value-rational approach recognizing teachers’ professional flourishing as an intrinsic good rather than an instrumental means.

items.title: Engagement in AI-Mediated Informal Digital Learning of English: An Adaptive Intelligence Perspective on Motivational, Psychological, and Technological Resources
items.abstract: Using adaptive intelligence as a theoretical lens, the study investigates how L2 motivational selves are associated with AI-IDLE engagement through psychological capital (PsyCap) and L2 grit and whether these indirect associations vary with AI literacy among 1025 Chinese university EFL learners. The proposed model was tested using structural equation modeling (SEM). For the ideal L2 self, associations with engagement emerged both directly and indirectly through PsyCap and L2 grit, whereas the ought-to L2 self showed an indirect association through PsyCap and no direct association with engagement. Higher AI literacy corresponded to stronger associations of both PsyCap and L2 grit with engagement. The two motivational self-guides were therefore associated with engagement through different psychological pathways, with AI literacy related to variation in the strength of these pathways. From an adaptive intelligence perspective, this conditional pattern indicates that the relevance of PsyCap and L2 grit to AI-IDLE engagement varies with learners’ AI literacy. These findings extend the application of adaptive intelligence to informal human–AI learning.

items.title: ENHANCING INTELLIGIBILITY AND LEARNER AUTONOMY IN EFL PRONUNCIATION INSTRUCTION THROUGH AI-DRIVEN PEDAGOGICAL FEEDBACK
items.abstract: Modern English as a Foreign Language (EFL) pronunciation instruction has shifted its primary goal from native-like accent imitation to functional intelligibility and comprehensibility. Despite this paradigm shift, traditional classroom settings often struggle to provide personalized, real-time diagnostic feedback due to large class sizes and time constraints. This study investigates the pedagogical integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven speech analysis and automated acoustic feedback in EFL pronunciation teaching. Synthesizing contemporary literature on Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT) and feedback literacy, this paper examines how AI feedback impacts learner autonomy, segmental clarity, and suprasegmental awareness. The review reveals that AI tools provide consistent, low-anxiety practice environments that facilitate cognitive noticing and self-correction. However, over-reliance on automated metrics without explicit pedagogical framing can result in mechanical practice detached from communicative contexts. To reconcile these dynamics, this article introduces a conceptual Scaffolded Pedagogical Feedback Model (SPFM) that integrates AI-generated acoustic diagnostic data, structured peer dialogue, and teacher-mediated instructional intervention. The framework highlights the necessity of developing student feedback literacy to transform automated output into actionable learning strategies. Keywords: EFL pronunciation instruction, Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT), artificial intelligence, intelligibility, learner autonomy, feedback literacy.

items.title: Epistemic Hidden Defects in Artificial Intelligence: Classical ʿIlal al-Ḥadīth as a Framework for AI Verification
items.abstract: This working paper examines whether the classical methodology of ʿilal al-Ḥadīth—the detection of hidden defects in apparently sound reports—can provide a useful conceptual framework for evaluating artificial-intelligence outputs in specialist knowledge environments. It develops the concept of the “epistemic hidden defect”: a weakness in provenance, attribution, inference, context, evidential hierarchy, or scholarly status that may remain concealed beneath a fluent and apparently authoritative AI-generated response. Drawing on classical Hadith-critical methodology and contemporary AI research, the paper distinguishes computational capability from scholarly authority. It develops the concepts of the Authority Ceiling, Digital Isnād, competence-specific human oversight, and the No-Autonomous-Grading Principle as safeguards for AI-assisted scholarship. The paper argues for an AI-assisted rather than AI-autonomous model of specialist research, in which computational systems widen the evidential field while consequential scholarly judgement remains traceable, reviewable, and accountable.

items.title: Estimating the threat of AI-agent responding across online survey platforms
items.abstract: Recent research and advances in LLMs have led to widespread concern that AI agents could pose as human online survey-takers. However, it remains unclear how prevalent AI agents are on survey research platforms and how to effectively detect AI agents. We validated a series of AI detection tests that effectively separated verified-human participants from both prompted commercial and purpose-built AI agents. Using these tests, we collected surveys on seven online platforms and find wide variation in rates of respondents failing AI tests, ranging from 6 to 41% across platforms (compared to a 2.4% false-positive rate for in-person human participants). We further demonstrate that undetected AI agents can impact the results of online surveys. Our findings suggest that while there is an urgent need for AI detection tests and consistent, systematic monitoring of data quality on online platforms, some platforms currently appear to provide data with a low rate of AI agents.
